analysis.one_liner: Requires chemical makers to prove their products are safe before selling them, and lets the EPA ban chemicals that fail.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in July 2005 with 7 Senate sponsors, it sat in the Environment and Public Works Committee until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the law at the time, chemical makers could sell most substances without ever showing they were safe. This bill would have flipped that: every manufacturer would have to certify, over the CEO's signature, that its chemicals meet a safety standard protecting children and workers, or admit the data is missing. The EPA would review the most dangerous 300 chemicals first and phase in reviews of everything else, banning substances that could not be shown safe, and create a public database of chemical toxicity.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, workers, and consumers exposed to untested chemicals. The bill's stated goal was to eliminate harmful chemical exposure by 2020, starting with a priority list of the 300 highest-risk substances and an extra 10-fold safety factor for infants and children. Workers and the public would also gain a right to know: a public database of chemical toxicity, biomonitoring of chemicals found in human blood, and public access to hazard data.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each manufacturer to submit a CEO-signed certification that its chemical meets a safety standard protecting fetuses, infants, children, workers, and other sensitive groups, or certify the data is insufficient — and to update it every three years or whenever new toxicity information emerges.

Bars the sale of any chemical that fails the safety standard, that a manufacturer refuses to comply for, or that EPA never gets to review on deadline — flipping the current system, where chemicals stay on the market by default.

The bill's findings state that EPA had reviewed the human health risks of only an estimated 2 percent of the 62,000 chemicals in use in 1976 and had banned or restricted just 5 substances in 29 years, because the existing law's hurdles were too high to clear.

Creates a public electronic database of chemical toxicity and exposure, requires biomonitoring studies of chemicals made in volumes over one million pounds a year, and requires manufacturers to publish a practical way to detect their chemicals in human blood and tissue.

Directs EPA to build market incentives for safer substitutes — expedited review and a public 'safer alternative' designation — and funds green chemistry research centers offering technical help to small and mid-sized manufacturers.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers, who would bear the cost of safety testing, biomonitoring studies, and certification for every chemical they sell — costs that could be passed to consumers through higher prices, or paid in products withdrawn from the market pending review.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden would fall on manufacturers: safety data for every chemical, biomonitoring studies every three years for high-volume substances, and CEO-signed certifications — costs likely to be passed on in prices and to fall hardest on smaller producers, though the bill funds green chemistry centers to help small and mid-sized firms.

The bill shifts the burden of proof, so a useful chemical could be pulled from commerce if a manufacturer cannot produce adequate safety data by the deadline — even if no one has shown the chemical is actually harmful. The bill itself acknowledges the disruption risk by letting the President grant five-year renewable exemptions where a chemical's absence would 'cause significant disruption in the national economy.'

EPA would have to make safety determinations for all chemicals in commerce within 15 years — an enormous workload for an agency whose record under the old law was reviewing roughly 2 percent of existing chemicals, raising the question of whether the deadlines were realistic.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: consumers and workers get a legal guarantee that chemicals sold to them have been shown safe for children, and chemical makers pay for the testing that guarantee requires. The bill was genuinely ambitious — a full reversal of the default in the 1976 Toxic Substances Control Act — and the concerns are about execution, not principle: whether EPA could meet the deadlines, whether missing data would strip useful products from shelves, and how much testing costs would reach consumers. Its exemptions for national security and economic disruption, and its funding for animal-testing alternatives, suggest an attempt to soften those costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Frank Lautenberg introduced the Kid Safe Chemicals Act on July 13, 2005, joined by six Senate cosponsors: Independent Jim Jeffords and Democrats Barbara Boxer, John Kerry, Jon Corzine, Hillary Clinton, and Edward Kennedy.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
That was the bill's last action: the full action history shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remaining year and a half of the Congress.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill expired without ever receiving a vote in committee or on the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers are better off: the existing system, under which most chemicals were never reviewed for safety before sale, stayed in place. The status quo that the bill's own findings described — EPA having reviewed about 2 percent of the chemicals on the market and banned only 5 in 29 years — continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical manufacturers, in the unreviewed status quo

for.name: Frank R. Lautenberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Barbara Boxer, John Kerry, Jon Corzine, Hillary Clinton, and Edward Kennedy

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. James Inhofe (R-OK)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill stayed in committee from July 2005 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Chemical manufacturing industry
against.role: Regulated industry facing new testing and certification mandates
against.what_they_did: Opposed overhauls of the Toxic Substances Control Act that would require premarket safety testing, in the broader decade-long debate over TSCA reform.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Republican with no recorded action.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to sell untested chemicals: every substance would need CEO-certified safety data, periodic biomonitoring, and an EPA determination, with sales banned where data is missing or safety is not shown. Those compliance costs are the flip side of the health protection the bill promises the public.
Mandatory safety data and biomonitoring studies for every chemical in commerce would create a large, sustained demand for testing services.

The bill funds green chemistry research centers, expedited review, and a public 'safer alternative' designation that firms could use in marketing, giving developers of non-toxic substitutes a market edge.
